source.summary: Marcus dines out about eight times a month at ~$70 a head and rotates three local favourites. Being known (his table, his partner's nut allergy) is why he returns; at a place that treats him as a stranger after ~30 visits he has quietly cut visits from monthly to quarterly. He wants a self-updated guest profile, would use an app only for places he visits often, is happy with SMS, and supports prime-slot deposits that are refundable, off the bill and waived for regulars.

nuggets.text: Marcus has dinner out about eight times a month and spends around $70 a head with wine.
nuggets.quote: I probably spend around seventy dollars a head on dinner, with wine.

nuggets.text: Marcus rotates three regular restaurants and has been to the Italian 40–50 times over four years.
nuggets.quote: I have three that I rotate.

nuggets.text: Marcus keeps going back because the staff know his table, his wine and his partner's nut allergy without being told.
nuggets.quote: Because they know me. That's the whole thing.

nuggets.text: The tapas place's manager sent a free birthday plate after seeing the date in their system, unprompted.
nuggets.quote: the manager once sent out a free plate for my birthday. I hadn't even mentioned it, they just saw it in their system.

nuggets.text: After about 30 visits the Japanese counter still asks Marcus whether he has been there before.
nuggets.quote: After thirty visits, I'm a stranger there. Every time I book they ask "have you been here before?"

nuggets.text: Feeling invisible, Marcus cut visits to the Japanese place from monthly to every three months without telling them.
nuggets.quote: I used to go there monthly, now it's every three months. I never told them why. People don't complain, they just drift.

nuggets.text: Marcus wants to log in once and record his partner's allergy so every booking carries it.
nuggets.quote: If I could log in somewhere and say, "Hey, my partner's allergy, here it is," then they'd have it for every booking, and I'd never repeat it.

nuggets.text: Repeating his partner's nut allergy to every restaurant, every time, is exhausting and a little scary.
nuggets.quote: I repeat the allergy thing every single time, to every restaurant, it's exhausting and a little scary.

nuggets.text: Marcus would like one app holding all his bookings and one profile across his three restaurants, not an app per restaurant.
nuggets.quote: Not an app per restaurant, one that has all my bookings.

nuggets.text: A link is perfect for a place visited twice a year, but for forty visits Marcus wants an app or at least an account.
nuggets.quote: If you go twice a year, a link is perfect. If you go forty times, give me an app. Or an account at least.

nuggets.text: Marcus uses one big booking platform app for upscale places, but it doesn't list his local independents.
nuggets.quote: I already use one big platform app for, you know, the fancy ones, and it's fine, but it doesn't have my little local places.

nuggets.text: Marcus books his Italian by texting the owner directly, the tapas place through its website widget and the Japanese counter by phone.
nuggets.quote: The Italian, I text the owner. Directly.

nuggets.text: After 30-plus bookings the tapas widget still makes Marcus type his name, email and phone every time.
nuggets.quote: Why am I typing my phone number? I'd like it to remember.

nuggets.text: The widget has no table-preference field, so Marcus writes it in notes and doesn't know if anyone reads them.
nuggets.quote: I have to add it in the notes, and I don't know if anyone reads the notes.

nuggets.text: Marcus reads his texts and likes an SMS reminder with 'reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel'.
nuggets.quote: I'm perfectly happy with SMS. I read my texts. A text with "Reply 1 to confirm, 2 to cancel", that's perfect for me.

nuggets.text: Marcus has no problem with a ~$20-per-head deposit on Friday or Saturday prime slots if it comes off the bill.
nuggets.quote: For a Friday or Saturday prime slot, absolutely, no problem.

nuggets.text: Deposits should be waived for known regulars like him and asked of strangers booking eight seats on a Saturday.
nuggets.quote: If I'm someone who's come forty times, don't ask me for a card. Ask the stranger who just booked eight seats on a Saturday.

nuggets.text: Marcus accepts a no-show fee only if clearly agreed at booking; an unseen $50 charge he would dispute with his card company.
nuggets.quote: Some places do it sneakily, that's what I hate. A fifty-dollar charge I'd not seen. That I would dispute with my card company.

nuggets.text: Marcus would pay $4–5 a month, no more, for guaranteed priority tables at his three places on busy nights.
nuggets.quote: If an app really gave me priority at my three places, like a guaranteed table on a busy night, I'd pay a few dollars a month. Four, five dollars. Not more.

nuggets.text: Marcus finds paying to be a regular weird; recognition should feel earned.
nuggets.quote: It's weird to pay to be a regular. It should feel earned.

nuggets.text: Points and punch cards don't motivate Marcus; he values recognition over discounts.
nuggets.quote: Honestly, points don't excite me. I'm not buying dinner to get a free coffee. What I like is not a discount, it's recognition.

nuggets.text: Regulars' knowledge lives in the 62-year-old owner's head and is lost when staff change; a system would keep it.
nuggets.quote: If it were in a system, it would stay. That's the point.

nuggets.text: When booking for his partner's birthday, Marcus wants the note to actually reach the table.
nuggets.quote: When I book for my partner's birthday, I'd love to add a note and have it actually reach the table.

nuggets.text: Marcus says remembering his partner's allergy alone is something he would pay for.
nuggets.quote: Remember my partner's allergy so I don't have to say it out loud. That alone I'd pay for, honestly.
